o: We must count ordered sequences of $k$ **positive** integers summing to $n$ whose product is even. The product is even iff **at least one** term is even, so the answer equals (all compositions) − (compositions where every part is odd). Example 1: all compositions of 5 into 3 parts is C(4,2)=6, odd-only ones are the three permutations of [1,1,3], giving 6−3=3. Example 2: C(2,1)=2 total, zero odd-only (3 can't be a sum of two odds... actually 1+... no two odds sum to odd 3 minus—two odds give even sum), so answer 2. Example 3: only [1,1,1,1,1] exists and it's odd, so 0. Constraints ($n$ up to 5·10^5) demand an $O(n)$ or $O(n \log MOD)$ solution via precomputed factorials.
k: Product parity depends only on whether any term is even, so answer = (#compositions of n into k parts) − (#compositions into k odd parts).
Compositions of n into k positive parts: stars and bars gives C(n−1, k−1).
Writing each odd part as 2yᵢ+1 shows odd-part compositions exist iff n−k is even, and then equal C((n−k)/2 + k − 1, k − 1).

a.n: Approach 1: Dynamic Programming over (sum used, parity seen)
a.i: Build sequences left to right tracking how much sum remains and whether an even element has been placed. dp[rem][e] counts completions. This directly mirrors the problem definition and is easy to reason about, though its $O(nk)$ time can be too slow at the largest constraints — it still passes moderate inputs and demonstrates correctness.
s: Define f(rem, len, e): ways to fill len more positive integers summing to rem, e = whether an even term was already placed.
Base case: len == 0 → valid iff rem == 0 and e == true.
Transition: try every value v in [1..rem], recurse with (rem−v, len−1, e OR v even).
Memoize on (rem, len, e); answer is f(n, k, false) mod 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n²k) states-times-transitions in the naive form above (O(nk) states, O(n) transition each) — instructive but too slow for n = 5·10^5.

a.n: Approach 2: Complementary Counting with Stars and Bars (Optimal)
a.i: All compositions of n into k positive parts number C(n−1, k−1). A composition has odd product iff every part is odd; substituting part = 2yᵢ+1 turns this into compositions of (n−k)/2 extra units into k nonnegative parts, i.e. C((n−k)/2 + k − 1, k − 1), which exists only when n−k is even. Subtracting gives the answer in closed form.
s: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n modulo 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n) — factorial precomputation dominates; each binomial is O(1).

w: In an interview, mention the DP briefly to show you understand the structure, then derive the closed form via complementary counting — it is the expected solution. Pitfalls: forgetting that parts must be positive (hence C(n−1,k−1), not C(n+k−1,k−1)); forgetting the parity condition (n−k even) for odd-only compositions; negative results after subtraction mod 1e9+7 (add MOD before reducing); overflow in C++/Java (use 64-bit intermediates). Edge cases: k = n (only all-ones sequence → answer 0 unless impossible since product odd), n = k = 1 (answer 0). Follow-ups: count sequences with odd product instead (just return oddOnly), or require product divisible by a prime p (needs inclusion–exclusion or generating functions).
